messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 46
- Gender: Non-binary
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Software Engineer
- Trauma Type: Police violence
- Pcl5: 54

**Patient Vignette: A Case of Police Violence and Its Aftermath**

The patient, a 46-year-old South Asian software engineer who uses they/them pronouns, sits forward in the chair, hands clasped tightly. They are a quiet, careful person by nature, they explain—someone who spends their days thinking in logic, in code, in clean lines of cause and effect. But what happened to them three years ago does not follow any logic, and they have been unable to make it fit.

The event occurred on a Tuesday evening in late autumn. They had been driving home from a client site, a long stretch of highway that cuts through the industrial outskirts of the city. A routine commute. They noticed the police lights in their rearview mirror, and their first thought was that they had left a turn signal on too long. They pulled over, turned off the engine, and placed their hands on the steering wheel as they had always been taught by their immigrant parents: be visible, be compliant, be safe.

The officer approached, asked for their license and registration. They provided it. They answered every question calmly, using the same measured tone they use in code reviews. But the officer’s demeanor shifted. He asked if they knew why he had stopped them. They did not. He asked if they were on something. They were not. Then, without warning, the officer yanked the door open and pulled them out of the car by their arm. They remember the asphalt scraping through their jeans, the weight of a knee on their back, the sound of their own voice—high, strange, not their own—saying, “Please, I’m just going home.”

The arrest was for “obstruction,” a charge later dropped. The physical injuries healed in weeks: a cracked rib, deep bruising along their spine. But the body remembers differently. For the first six months afterward, they could not drive. They took leave from work, then extended it. They would sit in the passenger seat while their spouse drove, and every time a police car appeared in the side mirror—even a block away, even in the opposite lane—their chest would seize, their hands would go numb, and they would hear themselves say, “Don’t stop. Please don’t stop.”

They returned to work after eight months, but the software engineering role that once felt like a sanctuary now feels like a trap. Open-plan offices mean people walking behind them, sudden movements in peripheral vision. They have moved their desk to a corner with a clear view of the door. They flinch when a colleague taps them on the shoulder. They cannot go to the company cafeteria because the fluorescent lights and the echoes of voices—too many voices, too many bodies—make them feel like they are back on that asphalt.

Their marriage has become a quiet, careful thing. Their spouse, a gentle person, has learned not to surprise them, not to approach from behind. The patient feels a deep, cold shame about this. They are supposed to be the steady one, the problem-solver. Now they spend nights awake, replaying the sequence of events, trying to find the variable they could have changed. Was it the way they held their hands? The tone of their voice? They run the code of that evening over and over, but the output never changes.

They have stopped going to protests, stopped reading the news, stopped talking to friends who ask about their life. They feel porous, as if the skin they live in has become a kind of accusation. At work, they are still competent, but their productivity has slipped. They avoid meetings, communicate through Slack, and have begun to wonder if they will ever feel safe again in a body that is so visible, so easily read as a threat.

The patient tells me all of this in a flat, precise voice, like they are describing a bug in a system that is not theirs. But when they finish, they look at me, and for the first time, their hands are still. “I don’t know how to un-see what I saw,” they say. “I don’t know how to un-feel what I felt.”
